question: What keeps a Qualcomm SoC out of its lowest state on mainline?
found: Any processor or bus vote left up: on a QCS8550 handheld, aosd, cxsd and ddr stayed at 0 until the USB controller's interconnect vote and the PCIe and LPASS (audio) votes were released, then it reached the floor at about 23 mA (2026-10). A DSP that never sleeps holds CX up; on surya the audio DSP has not slept once. FastRPC helpers attached across suspend crash the audio DSP: postmarketOS stops hexagonrpcd's helper before suspend on the Pixel 3a, as we saw on surya (24 of 24 attempts with rootpd attached). Wi-Fi (ath10k) floods the modem's IPC interrupt and blocks or breaks suspend on SDM845; surya is reported to wake at random while asleep, cause unknown.

question: How does a Qualcomm phone reach its lowest power state on mainline?
found: Through s2idle and CPU idle, not suspend to RAM: the firmware offers no PSCI system suspend, so with userspace frozen the CPUs enter their idle states, the last one down takes the cluster power domain to its deepest state (PSCI OS-initiated mode, hierarchical CPU idle), and as the cluster powers off the application processor's RPMh sleep votes are flushed to the always-on subsystem (rpmh-rsc attached to the cluster domain). The always-on subsystem then lowers CX and DDR when no processor votes for them: CX collapse (cxsd), then AOSS sleep (aosd), the floor. The SoC counts each in its own memory (rpmh-stats, read through qcom_stats), so reaching the floor is measured, not inferred. Without OS-initiated mode the cluster domain would stay always on and the votes would never flush; surya's firmware has it.

question: How does a Qualcomm phone on mainline wake for a call or a message?
found: The modem's messages (QMI over QRTR on glink) are handled even in s2idle (IRQF_NO_SUSPEND), but userspace is frozen, so nothing rings. The kernel cannot tell a call from a signal-strength update: there is one switch, the IPCRTR glink device's wakeup (/sys/bus/rpmsg/devices/4080000.remoteproc:glink-edge.IPCRTR.-1.-1/power/wakeup), which wakes for every modem message. postmarketOS (now Nura) pairs it on the OnePlus 6 with ModemManager's quick suspend/resume, which quiets the modem's notifications before suspend and resyncs after; that fixed calls signalled late or lost. It is still not dependable: on OnePlus 6/6T and the Pixel 3a waking for calls is reported not working (with the switch on the phone wakes at once; open since 2026-10), and with it on every modem event wakes the phone. surya's modem sits at the same address (remoteproc 4080000), so the same path applies; a SIM card is needed to prove it.

question: How else have phones got deep sleep that still rings?
found: Android's own kernel: Ubuntu Touch runs officially on surya through Halium with the vendor's 4.14 kernel and Android's opportunistic suspend (wakeup sources and autosleep, which mainline also has), claiming a day and more - deep sleep that works, at the price of the vendor's kernel and blobs and nothing upstream. A separate power-management core: Crust on the PinePhone sleeps the whole Allwinner SoC (about 80% less power) and the separate modem wakes it through its RI line; Qualcomm's always-on subsystem runs signed firmware, so nothing like Crust can be written for it, and its modem is inside the SoC. Push through sleep: only partly solved anywhere (PinePhone: WoWLAN pattern matching plus an RTC wake as a safety net). The postmarketOS SM7150 page lists suspend as working with no measurement behind it; we found no published standby current for mainline Qualcomm phones.

question: Does sm7150's device tree ask the firmware for the cluster states surya's firmware knows?
found: Apparently not, for the two deepest. sm7150.dtsi (sm7150-mainline, the same in our tree) carries three cluster states whose latencies are surya's own but whose PSCI parameters are SC7180's: 0x41000044 (cluster power collapse), 0x41001244 and 0x4100b244. surya's own Android device tree (lpm-levels, cluster mode shifted by 4) has l3-pc 0x4, cx-off 0x224 and llcc-off 0xc24 - that is 0x41000044, 0x41002244 and 0x4100c244; 0x4100c244 is also what SM8150, the closest sibling, uses for its one cluster sleep. On the phone the deepest state (0x4100b244) was never entered once at runtime. Whether the firmware rejects, demotes or honours SC7180's values is not known: it is the first thing a measured suspend settles. SM7150 is not yet in mainline: the 2025 upstreaming series is to be resent, so a correction can go into it.

question: Where does surya's deep sleep stand, measured on the phone itself?
found: Measured 2026-11-17 on the test kernel 7.1.0-rc3-sm7150-wcd, read only. The kernel offers only s2idle, as on every Qualcomm phone. PSCI 1.1 runs in OS-initiated mode, and the CPU and cluster idle states are in use at runtime. The SoC's own sleep counters are readable (qcom_stats, from rpmh-stats at 0xc3f0000). Since boot: no suspend at all (suspend_stats success 0 - on USB the lab holds devlab-usb, and Sxmo holds sxmo_not_suspendable and sxmo_modem_warming_up); CX collapse (cxsd) 0, AOSS sleep (aosd) 0, DDR low-power states 0; the deepest cluster state (cluster-sleep-2) never entered once while the lighter two were entered thousands of times. The audio DSP never slept (adsp 0) while the compute DSP and the modem slept about 200 times each; no audio stream was open, yet the VA, TX and RX macros stayed active, and the command line carries soundwire_qcom.stay_awake=1 from the microphone hunt. So no measurement of deep sleep exists yet, and two things already seen would keep the SoC from its floor.

question: What already exists for measuring a phone's health on the phone, shipping it there, and letting agents work with it - in postmarketOS and in our own commons?
found: postmarketOS (docs.postmarketos.org/pmaports/main/ci/hardware-ci.html): tests ship as small shell files in postmarketos-test-* packages (suspend by an RTC wake alarm; bootrr, which checks per board, keyed by the device tree's compatible, that every expected driver probed) and run in the initramfs CI hook on their hardware CI (CI-tron gateway); surya has no bootrr board file yet. In the commons: the package conveyor (linux-package-distribution-oco/conveyor) already builds static aarch64-musl binaries with signed provenance and plans signed Alpine repositories for postmarketOS (cv-apk) and machines that receive updates, the phone next (cv-machines-refresh); agent access (creation-guidelines/agent-access-oco) plans every tool's structured door offered over MCP, in Rust with rmcp, naming devlab among the first (aa-two-doors). In lab-tools itself: devlab test ran surya's checks from the lab over SSH, health kept a baseline of what ever passed, watch ran health after each boot from the lab - nothing ran on the phone by itself, and the checks were one surya-specific file.

question: How can calls, messages and data be checked without a person?
found: Data checks itself: a small download over the mobile connection. A call needs someone to answer: a second phone on a test stand that answers and confirms, or a programmable telephone number that answers and plays a known tone the phone can hear. Until then, half-manual: the phone calls a person's number and the person confirms through the inbox.

question: Why does nothing come back from surya's main microphone, now that the WCD9375 enumerates and the sound card is made?
found: The codec dropped off both SoundWire buses because ASoC puts every idle component into its sleep pin state, and the codec's sleep state drove its active-low reset low (traced: snd_soc_bind_card committed it 0.24 ms before both interfaces went UNATTACHED). Without a sleep state the codec stays attached and capture prepares (linux-phone-oco/linux PR #4); the SoundWire pin-mux fix is PR #3. Capture still yields exact zeros: the built-in microphones are digital mics (vendor: TX DMIC1-3 on LPI gpio26-29, function 1, mic bias 1 and 3); this ADSP rejects the VA capture port, so they go through the TX macro to TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3; with the VA DMIC clocks forced on the TX path still reads zeros, as it does from ADC1 - the next fault sits in the TX decimator to DSP leg. Details: research/microphone.md.

question: Why does the modem not go online once a SIM card is in?
found: With the SIM in (operator 1&1, card present and ready) the modem refuses every request to go online: its own operating mode reads shutting-down from the start of boot, and ModemManager gets DeviceNotReady. The modem processor boots cleanly; rmtfs and tqftpserv run; the kernel's pd-mapper module is loaded. Meanwhile the modem reads and writes /readwrite/lctoem.tmp over tqftpserv in an endless loop, with rsize=0 seek=0 options, each read ending at once - the same kind of loop that postmarketOS fixed for the Fairphone 4 and 5 with a tqftpserv that handles rsize and seek. A reboot with the SIM in place changed nothing.

question: What does the community report for surya, and where does it disagree with what our checks measure?
found: Of 19 parts, 9 agree. The wiki reports calls, SMS and NFC working where our checks say unknown (no SIM card yet); mobile data and Bluetooth working where we measured partial; the speaker partial where we measured it working; and the sensors working where we measured broken - possibly our own doing, since we masked the sensor service to stop the audio processor crashing on suspend. The claims were gathered earlier, on an unrecorded date; this comparison is of today.

question: How do SM6150/SM7150 'bolero' boards and their siblings (SM7125 atoll, SM6115 bengal, QCS615 talos) record their microphones on mainline and open stacks, and what does the vendor's own model say?
found: Working on mainline, legacy q6afe firmware: SM7150 davinci (sm7150-mainline PR 60, open, -62 dBFS floor) and surya (pulpoff/linux-surya; and linux-phone-oco since 2026-11-17), both through analog mics on the WCD9375 -> TX SoundWire -> TX macro DEC (SWR_MIC) -> TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3. The SM7150-specific trap: its TX SoundWire controller has one dout port, which shifts both the master port numbers (inputs from port 2) and the controller's DAIs (capture is DAI 1); SM7125, the template, has none, so its <&swr2 0> is right there. Nobody streams the VA port on SM6150/SM7150; both trees declare a VA link and leave out the DCODEC vote this ADSP refuses. The vendor (sm6150 bolero, qcom,va-without-decimation) uses the VA block only for MCLK, the fs counter and DMIC clocks, clocked from the TX macro's MCLK through bolero's mclk mux, and routes every TX and RX path to VA_MCLK; mainline gives the same through the VA macro's fsgen clock on the TX macro. No open implementation of va-without-decimation exists - only a board with real DMICs on this family would need it. SM6115/QRB4210 (Linaro RB2 v3) records DMICs through VA_CODEC_DMA_TX_0 with the DCODEC vote: not a template here. QCS615 upstream (2026-05) is AudioReach with an external DA7212, headset mic only. postmarketOS ships no microphone support for SM7150 (wiki: N, UCM speaker-only).

question: Which microphones does surya have, and on which inputs?
found: Two built-in analog microphones on the WCD9375: the bottom one on AMIC1 (mic bias 1) into ADC1, the top one on AMIC3 (mic bias 3) into ADC2 with its input mux at INP3; the headset mic is AMIC2 (bias 2) on the same ADC2 at INP2. ADC1 comes back over the TX SoundWire bus on master port 2, ADC2 needs its own master port 3 (qcom,tx-port-mapping <2 3 4 5>): sharing port 2 with ADC1 lost the top mic and turned the bottom one to full-scale noise (pulpoff). No digital mics: pulpoff names LPI gpio7-11 NC, among them gpio8-11, the DMIC clock and data pins (vendor gpio26-29), and records both mics through ADC1/ADC2 on mainline. The TX DMIC1-3 routes read on 2026-11-17 come from sdmmagpie-qrd-overlay.dts, Qualcomm's QRD reference board kept in Xiaomi's tree, which declares the SWR_ADC0/ADC2 routes beside them. Measured on the phone (bring-up, 2026-11-17 04:37 UTC, test/surya-mic with <&swr2 1>): mic-records pass and mic-hears-speaker pass, a 1 kHz tone at -19.4 dBFS against -76.3 dBFS of noise through ADC1. The DMIC experiment (pins at mux 1, VA DMIC clocks on a switch) answered a question surya does not ask and is to be dropped.

question: What made the TX decimator to codec DMA path deliver zeros, and what does a capture of zeros tell?
found: The decimator-to-DSP leg worked all along: each silent recording began with ~0.5 s of ringing (-1774 settling to exact 0), the high-pass filter draining a constant input - the decimator ran and its output reached TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3, but no samples entered it. The cause was upstream of the decimator: the capture link named the TX SoundWire controller's DAI 0, its playback DAI (qcom_swrm_register_dais makes the first num_dout_ports DAIs playback, and this controller has one dout port), so sdw_stream_add_master was never called and the codec's ports never programmed. The same one-dout-port shift moves master port numbers by one (ports start at 2; swr2's qcom,ports-* arrays begin with 0xff). For DMICs the same reading held: with no clock on the pin the data line is static and the filter removes it. So: start-up ringing then exact zeros means no input reaches the decimator - look at the source (SoundWire stream, DMIC clock), not the DMA or the AFE port. The AFE port is the vendor's too: TX AIF1 on TX_CDC_DMA_TX_3 (45111 = 0xB037), accepted by this ADSP.

question: Which public number can an automated call reach from a German mobile, that plays back what it hears, free or at the national rate?
found: Only one German public echo line is attested across sources and years: blueSIP's echo test, +49 89 721010 99701, a Munich landline number (landline rate: inside any German allnet flat, about 9 ct/min on plain prepaid), named in forums in 2005 and 2013, recommended in 2021, and still on Placetel's list (which gives no warranty). It plays back what it hears at once (an echo, not record-then-playback); no length limit is stated. The same provider's +49 89 721010 99702 plays a signal tone: a downlink-only control that needs no working uplink. sipgate's echo (10005) and test (10000) are SIP-internal short codes, not dialable from a mobile, and sipgate serves only business customers since 2025-06. Other European lines (portunity's 0211 237099929 from 2005, sip2sip's +31 20 8005161, a Dutch C*NET echo) are old and unconfirmed, and abroad costs more. No source confirms any line works from a mobile today, so the first supervised call settles it. Fallback that is certain to exist and free on German tariffs: the SIM's own mailbox (record a message, play it back by DTMF; slower and operator-specific).

question: What does a voice call with sound both ways need on surya, and what is there now?
found: Read on the phone 2026-11-17 (devlab phone sh, read only): the modem is online now - LTE on Vodafone.de (26202), registered home, packet service attached, signal 71%, UE mode csps-1, voice-centric with PS (VoLTE) preferred, so a call goes VoLTE if the modem's IMS profile allows it, else falls back to GSM; ModemManager 1.25.95, libqmi 1.38, tqftpserv 1.3, rmtfs 1.3; callaudiod and q6voiced are installed; no calls listed. The kernel (7.1.0-sm7150-mic+, linux-phone-oco/linux test/surya-mic) has no VoiceMMode PCM and no Voice Mixer controls: q6voice is not in it. pulpoff/linux-surya (7.2.15 on surya) carries calls with audio both ways: q6voice from sdm845-mainline (MVM, CVS, CVP over APR) with the CVD 2.3 set-up SM7150 needs (from the CVP version), codec DMA ports, a zeroed command buffer and the start moved from startup to prepare; the device tree adds the APR services and a hostless VoiceMMode1 link (PCM 4, hw:0,4) that q6voiced opens per call; routing 'TERT_MI2S_RX Voice Mixer VoiceMMode1' and 'VoiceMMode1 Capture Mixer TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3' (our kernel uses the same back-end names); 'VoiceMMode1 TX Topology' at 0x10F70 (none) since the default 0x10F71 sends silence without Xiaomi's calibration; and the uplink is silent unless a 1-channel capture runs on TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3 for the whole call (their surya-call-uplink on MultiMedia3; 2 channels or a prepared-only stream do not do). callaudiod picks a UCM Voice Call verb (earpiece or speaker). The order: q6voice and the device tree first (the PCM and controls appear - check call-audio-path), then UCM Voice Call with the topology and the uplink capture, then a call.

question: How can the phone itself decide that a call carried sound both ways?
found: Acoustically, through the paths a person uses, with the analysis in Rust: during the call the uplink capture that the call needs anyway (1 channel on TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3, the bottom mic) is written to a file instead of thrown away. The phone plays a pattern of three short tones (e.g. 800, 1300, 1900 Hz, 200 ms each, 300 ms apart - inside the 300-3400 Hz every voice codec keeps) on the loudspeaker at the manifest's quiet level; the bottom mic hears it at once (proves the injection) and sends it up the call; the echo comes back down and plays on the earpiece, and the same mic hears it again 150-1500 ms later (the network's round trip; acoustic reflections are under 20 ms). A Goertzel envelope per frequency finds the pattern twice; the echo counts when the same order of tones recurs at one delay, 15 dB above the noise, and the delay is reported. Before the echo call, a call to the tone line (99702) proves the downlink alone, so a missing echo says uplink (or the line) rather than everything. Cost: one call of at most 25 s (dial, about 8 s to answer, 5 s of pattern, hang up; a hard timeout), at most once a day, a landline-rate number: inside a flat, or under 10 ct per day on prepaid. Skips cleanly, as unknown: no modem, no SIM, not registered, no voice interface, no call path (call-audio-path failing), the daily call already made, or the number unset in the manifest. A pass proves works for modem-calls. If q6voice exposes in-call record/playback ports (downstream's VOICE_RECORD_RX, incall music), a digital loop could replace the acoustic one later; unknown on this driver.

question: How should the phones' health suites be organised to cover every part and feature, stay quick to change and dependable, and avoid Python?
found: What is: devlab-health, a static Rust runner (lab-tools/health), runs shell checks on the phone after every boot in two layers (base, shell): 11 generic in lab-tools and 5 of surya's own in surya-lab; each prints 'pass|fail|skip TEST COMPONENT detail' and docs' tests table says what each pass proves. The weak spot is computation in shell: three of surya's checks carry a Goertzel filter written in awk and a tone made byte by byte with printf, because lab-tools' tested tone crate never reaches the phone. The phone has no Rust toolchain (it has python3, which the lab refuses), so rust-script (stable, 0.36 on the lab) cannot run there and would need a toolchain and network on the phone; Cargo's own single-file scripts (frontmatter, cargo PR 16569) are still nightly-only in Cargo 1.99. KTAP is the kernel's test output (ok/not ok, SKIP, nested suites) - a format our lines map onto if LAVA-style tools are ever wanted. Shape that fits: shell stays for what is a reading (sysfs, a command's output; ten readable lines), and anything with numbers, timing or a state machine (tones, echoes, calls, sleep counters) is a subcommand of one static multi-call Rust binary shipped with devlab-health (e.g. devlab-health tone find, devlab-health call echo), built with its unit tests and recorded fixtures on the lab and cross-built by health/build.sh; rust-script is the lab's prototyping and one-off analysis tool against recordings fetched from the phone, a prototype becoming a subcommand once it is kept. Coverage is read off the data: a query of every device's components with no test that proves works, and a layer per cost - base, shell, then telephony (calls and data, gated by budget and once a day) and witnessed (needs a person).

question: How can mobile data be checked after every boot within about 3 GB?
found: Per run: the modem registered and its bearer connected (mmcli), the bearer's interface found from ModemManager, then over that interface only (curl --interface, so Wi-Fi cannot pass for it): a DNS lookup, five pings to a fixed address (round trip, loss), and a 100 kB HTTPS download timed (speed.cloudflare.com/__down?bytes=100000 or a file the project hosts), about 150 kB with overheads. Boots run up to ~45 a day in bring-up, so about 7 MB on a heavy day; once a week a 5 MB download measures throughput. That is under 0.3 GB a month even on busy months: the 3 GB lasts most of a year at the worst rate and years at an ordinary one. A check also reads the bearer's own byte counters (the interface's /sys/class/net/IFACE/statistics before and after) so each run states what it used, and skips when the month's total passes a budget set in the manifest. Skips without a SIM, as the modem checks already do.

question: Why did surya's modem fail as soon as a SIM went in, and what makes mobile data work?
found: The modem looped 4769 times reading and writing /readwrite/lctoem.tmp: tqftpserv 1.1.1 (Alpine v3.24) never writes short WRQ files, so the state files stayed 0 bytes, the modem stayed in DMS mode shutting-down, UIM reported 'GW primary session index unknown' and ModemManager 'sim-missing'. tqftpserv 1.3 from Alpine edge (two packages, no other dependencies) fixed it on the next boot: mode online, Vodafone.de LTE, home registration, signal 71%. Mobile data then failed with 'Multiple PDN connection to same APN not allowed' when the NetworkManager connection named the APN web.vodafone.de: the modem's default profile attaches with an empty APN, which the network fills in. A gsm connection with no APN works: IPv4 and IPv6, 3/3 pings at 32 ms, 500 kB at 1.2 MB/s. The SIM sits in slot 2 (slot 1: no ATR), as pmaports #4441 found.

question: Should linux-phone-oco keep standing expert sessions, one per hard domain (audio, modem, sleep...), with the orchestrator routing questions to them - or keep expertise somewhere else?
found: The world has tried it under several names - specialised workers under a supervisor, hierarchical teams, blackboard systems, stateful agents - and converges on one split: the expert is a role and a body of written knowledge; a session is a disposable worker that takes the role up. Gas Town says it outright (an agent is a persistent identity, sessions are cattle; any session can hand off and restart from its hook). Anthropic's long-running harness found compaction alone not enough and had every fresh session get up to speed from a progress file, git and a feature list; its context-engineering guide names notes outside the window as the tool for iterative work with milestones. Claude Code itself moved this way: subagents may keep a per-role MEMORY.md, and agent teams start each teammate from project context and a spawn prompt, never the lead's history, and do not restore teammates on resume. Against expertise held in a long context: models recall worse as input grows (Chroma, context rot; Anthropic's attention budget), repeated summarising erodes detail (ACE: context collapse, brevity bias), and a session of 1000-1800 messages re-reads all of it each turn - after an idle hour without the cache, at full price - so a standing expert answering an occasional question is the costliest and not the most reliable way to answer it. Against a central router: a supervisor that relays every message plays telephone - lower scores and more tokens than agents handing off directly (LangChain); misalignment between agents (lost context, withheld information) is one of the three failure groups in 1600 traces (MAST). What works (Cognition, 2026): one writer per thing, other agents adding intelligence not actions; a consult works best given a fork of the asker's full context. Blackboard systems route by a shared record agents read, not by a relay. For us: most of the audio expertise is already rows in docs (5 research, 2 decisions, 27 backlog items name the microphone); what is not written is the tacit part - dead ends, where the experiment patches are, what hung the phone - and it now lives in hand-over notes outside any repository.

question: How do open practice and agent makers organise a knowledge base so that people and agents reach what they need without reading all of it?
found: They agree. (1) One small entry that is always read and routes onward, saying what each target is for: llms.txt, the root AGENTS.md (nearest wins), PhotoCraft's Read/Why orientation table, Johnny.Decimal's index, datapackage.json. (2) What is always loaded is kept small: CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, no more than ten per level, llms.txt's skippable Optional. (3) Detail in stages: Skills' name and line, then body, then linked files; Claude Code loads nested CLAUDE.md only when its subtree is touched; context engineering keeps lightweight identifiers - paths, stored queries - and loads content just in time. (4) Small units with stable addresses: evergreen notes whose titles work like APIs, numbered ADRs, Wikidata's Q and P ids. (5) Facts apart from explanation: Diátaxis' reference against explanation, Wikidata statements and infoboxes beside prose. (6) One decision per record, superseded rather than deleted (Nygard, MADR). (7) Every statement is about an item by its id and cites who says so (Wikidata). (8) Views are generated from the source data (PhotoCraft's scorecard, Mintlify's llms.txt). Tensions: hierarchy against association (fixed buckets vs dense links - a small fixed index with free links beneath answers both); one file against many (concatenation does not save context; loading on demand does). No source measured how much any of it speeds an agent - the measure here is docs' own (kb-navigation-measured).

question: How much must an agent read in docs today to answer a typical question, and what would an entry and a link cut it to?
found: Measured on main 2026-11-17 (bytes; about 4 per token). What is known of surya's microphone: there is no checked link from a record to what it is about - research, backlog and session_log have no such field, and decisions' about is free text in four spellings (microphone, features:microphone, linux-phone-oco/docs/features:microphone, a milestone id) and empty on 12 of 38. So an agent reads pages - research, decisions, backlog, support_status, feature_support: 206 KB, about 52k tokens - or greps data/ (79 KB of matched rows, noisy). The answer itself is 18 rows, 9.4 KB, about 2.3k tokens: 22 times less, but only reachable today by knowing the ids. What to do next on the modem: the backlog page is 84 KB (21k tokens); tad q backlog prints 327 KB in its box format (37 KB as csv) for all places; the answer is 2 open items, under 0.2 KB - found today only by matching words in titles. How to record a decision: tad statements answers it with every parameter in 3.5 KB (0.9k tokens), and practice 42 says it at session start - this one is already good. The entries: AGENTS.md (7 KB) is how to edit the data (setup, rules, recipes), not where knowledge is; README names 6 of 29 tables; the rendered index lists tables by count. Every session also reads 21 KB at start (practices and inbox). The rendered pages are 1.46 MB in all, 1 MB of them test_results. So the weight is not the entry files but the lack of a subject link: with an about link checked on every record table and a query about SUBJECT, the first two questions are one call of 2-10 KB.

question: What in the commons already does part of an ideal knowledge base, and would idealkb be one nature under a second name?
found: tad (creation-guidelines/tad-engine) is the engine: tables declared as data after Frictionless Table Schema, checked rows, canonical files, SQL, named queries and records with their header line as their description (tad statements is already an index of every question and record a base keeps). text-as-data-template is the template for a base kept as tad data - the same nature as idealkb - and has drifted: last changed 2026-11-04, still the vendored Python engine on a DuckDB schema that every base left on 2026-11-11 (as the vendored engines had drifted, three of four behind). ideal-project-playbook is how to run a software project - the loop, guards, CI, honesty - whose own docs/ is a tad base; its kit/templates for backlog, development log and idea page are records a base keeps as tables, and its findability test (real questions, the answer within the first three) is the measure a base needs. software-engineering-canon is a base itself (the spike the template came from). ideal-agent (grenudi/ideal-agent, 2026-11-17) is how agents work: practices, skills, hooks, and its own tad base; it keeps only what is general and leaves a project's domain in the project's data. ocoeco's marks (oco.toml exports, holds) and lenses say how a base fits the observatory's picture - its face, not its organisation. linux-phone-oco/docs is one tad base for every linux-phone place (2026-11-17-one-database), with prompts/ (role briefs), research/ (long prose), and rendered docs/ the face reads. Overlap: idealkb would be text-as-data-template under a second name; nothing else holds how knowledge is organised. Gap: no base links a record to what it is about, and no base has an entry that routes questions to queries.

question: Why does the ADSP sensors service crash-loop the audio DSP on surya, and what would stop it without changing the firmware?
found: Measured on the phone (read only, kept kernel 7.1.0-sm7150-calls+, 2026-11-17) and read in hexagonrpcd's source. At start the DSP's registry sensor compares each config it knows (the registry's sns_reg_config: 47 configs, every one recorded with data 1230768000 - 2009-01-01, Android's fixed vendor mtime) with the config files hexagonrpcd serves, and hexagonrpcd passes their real mtime: all 46 on the phone carry 1779945838 (the package's build time), and sns_pickup.json is listed but absent. Every config therefore looks changed, the DSP re-parses and writes (temp.json), hexagonrpcd refuses every write by design, and the DSP asserts (SNS_REG_INIT, sns_registry_sensor.c) and restarts with audio. The version marker sns_reg_version, whose absence also forces a rebuild elsewhere (hexagonrpc #19), cannot be served at all: the virtual persist/sensors/registry holds only its registry subdirectory. So no trial of 2026-11-09 had both conditions of an untouched registry - the marker reached and the configs unchanged; they disproved only a registry swap. Hypothesis to settle first: configs touched to 1230768000 (and no listed config missing) make the pre-parsed registry current, so nothing is written and the ADSP stays up. Independent of it: the same assert is open upstream on X1P42100 (#29, 2026-11-14) and was stopped by writes elsewhere (#19, #27).

question: Which sensors does surya carry, where, and is in-call proximity a real sensor?
found: All on the audio DSP's sensor core (no SLPI on SM7150), none on a bus Linux drives: the motion chip (accelerometer+gyroscope; one of bmi220, bmi26x, icm4x6xx, lsm6dso, probed by the DSP - the wiki names BMI220) on SPI instance 3; magnetometer AK09918 (ak0991x) on I2C 1 at 0x0c; adux1050, a capacitive SAR sensor for radio power, on I2C 1 at 0x2c (not the call proximity); Sensortek stk3a5x ambient light + infrared proximity on I2C 5 at 0x46, polled, near/far 12000/10000, one calibration value differing by panel (huaxing 2.0, tianma 1.0, chosen on Android by ro.boot.lcmtype through an apps-side get_property hexagonrpcd does not implement; the pre-parsed registry already holds stk3a5x). In-call proximity is that physical IR sensor: surya's tree has none of the ultrasound parts its sibling sweet carries (elliptic, mius, ro.vendor.audio.us), so the microphones and earpiece are not involved. The phone runs libssc 0.4.3 with ssccli, iio-sensor-proxy 3.9 with ssc support, and its udev tags fastrpc-adsp ssc-light, ssc-compass, ssc-accel, ssc-proximity; iio-sensor-proxy starts and waits ('registry sensor unavailable'). The suite's motion-and-light counted IIO devices only, so it could never pass through the sensor core.

question: Can the sensors helper stay attached across suspend, and what brings it back after?
found: postmarketOS stops sensorspd and rootpd before suspend (the units Conflicts=suspend.target; !5400 on the Pixel 3a, carried to systemd in !7303) and nothing restarts them: Restart=always does not fire on a conflict stop, by design - the helper is thought needed only while the DSP asks for its registry, and libssc talks QMI to the sensor service, not through hexagonrpcd. So after a first suspend on surya the sensors would have no helper; whether they keep working without it is unmeasured. One data point (SG6275P, #19) has a sensors helper with a writable registry surviving a 15 s rtcwake. surya's rootpd crash on suspend (24 of 24) is a separate helper; rootpd stays masked. No kernel fastrpc fix for suspend was found in 2025-2026; Qualcomm said in 2026-04 that a daemon attaching to a PD crashes the privileged PD and is being investigated.

question: Does surya's SoC reach its sleep floor in one measured s2idle on the kept kernel 7.1.0-sm7150-calls+?
found: No. One 60 s cycle by hand (USB gadget let go via soft_connect, rtcwake -m freeze -s 60, run as a transient systemd unit so it survives the link dropping; nohup in the ssh session is killed on exit). The phone slept the whole time: the pm8xxx_rtc_alarm interrupt fired once and suspend_stats success went 0 to 1, fail 0. The 2.4 s between the kernel log's suspend entry and exit, and between date readings, is only the clocks not counting sleep (monotonic and wall time stand still in s2idle here) - read the sleep from the RTC, not from date or dmesg. qcom_stats: cxsd 0, aosd 0, ddr 0 before and after; adsp never counted a sleep, cdsp 58, modem +7. Cluster domain: S1 usage 9417 to 9482 across the run, S2 (the deepest state) never entered. The suite's soc-sleeps now says fail: suspended, yet the SoC never reached its lowest state: cxsd 0, aosd 0; suspends this boot: 1; processors never asleep: adsp; wake locks: devlab-usb (devlab-health 20261117-115521). No hands needed: the phone woke by itself on the RTC alarm and came back over USB. Careful: reading /sys/power/wakeup_count blocks while a wakeup event is held (the lab's devlab-usb wake lock) - never read it without a timeout.

brief: surya's suspend ends at once: the serial's IRQ 157 (a storm, wake-armed) wakes s2idle; Bluetooth dies after it
question: Why does surya's s2idle end after about 2 s instead of 60, and what does the first measured cycle show?
found: Five cycles by hand (kept kernel 7.1.0-sm7150-calls+, one with the cluster parameters of surya's own firmware tables in the device tree) all end early: the RTC advanced a few seconds only, the suspend core goes from dpm_suspend_noirq end to dpm_resume_noirq begin in microseconds and the CPUs never enter s2idle's idle loop. A function trace names the wake: s2idle_wake <- pm_system_irq_wakeup <- irq_pm_handle_wakeup, during suspend_device_irqs, no wakeup source involved. The interrupt is IRQ 157, qcom_geni_serial_isr (the serial at 88c000, wake-enabled, count 200579 ten minutes after boot): the kernel logs 'irq 157: nobody cared' and disables it. So the cluster sleep parameters and the audio DSP cannot be judged yet: the SoC has not been let sleep once. Also seen: a suspend leaves Bluetooth hci0 dead (command tx timeout, Reading QCA version information failed -110) and pm_suspend hangs in hci_resume_dev for minutes - a reboot was needed. The soc-sleeps check says fail (suspends 1, cxsd 0, aosd 0, adsp never asleep). The earlier note that the phone slept the full 60 s was wrong: it read the RTC alarm interrupt count, which fires awake too.

brief: IRQ 157 is the Bluetooth UART; with it blocked, a timed s2idle cycle hung the phone hard (no way back on USB).
question: What holds IRQ 157 up in surya's s2idle, and what does a timed cycle do once Bluetooth is blocked?
found: IRQ 157 is the Bluetooth UART: GICv3 hwirq 636 = serial@88c000 (interrupts 0x25c), with hci0 UP RUNNING on it (TX 444 KB, 1847 commands); the console UART ttyMSM0 is a88000, a different device with no wakeup attribute. With bluetooth rfkill-blocked, one timed cycle (soft_connect 0, rtcwake -m freeze -s 60, run as transient unit cycle1) did NOT return: the phone showed the pmOS initramfs gadget (18d1:d001) with no network until the author force-rebooted it (vol-down+power). The previous boot's journal ends at 12:37:25, the cycle script and its log are not on disk, suspend_stats this boot 0/0: so the phone went down hard right at suspend entry, losing the last seconds, and its wake path (the PMIC RTC reads 1970, epoch 1280063 s) did not bring it back. Not known yet: whether the hang is the RTC alarm not waking s2idle, a crash entering s2idle with the audio DSP up, or a reset; and whether the IRQ-157 wake was cured. Health after reboot: healthy, 36 pass, 0 fail. Next try needs a way back not depending on USB networking: a hardware watchdog or timed reboot, the RTC set first, a log written to a place that survives (sync, pstore/ramoops or a serial console).

brief: surya has the qcom_wdt watchdog, 4 MiB ramoops and a PMIC RTC (1970); the stock watchdog is stopped in late suspend, so no way back covers a hang inside s2idle
question: What does surya have, and what do mainline and others do, for a way back from a suspend that may not return?
found: On the phone: qcom_wdt (17c10000.watchdog) with /dev/watchdog0, ramoops 4 MiB reserved at 0x9d800000 with pstore (console 1 MiB), the PMIC RTC reading 1970 and settable with hwclock -w -u; the kernel has no suspend timeout of its own (no PM_DEBUG, hung-task, DPM watchdog). Mainline qcom-wdt.c registers late system sleep ops that STOP an active watchdog in suspend and start it on resume: so a hang before the late phase is covered by a watchdog, one inside s2idle is not. A module with that stop made optional (one parameter, no other change) builds for the running kernel (no MODVERSIONS; vermagic equals uname -r) and loads without a kernel rebuild or reboot-to-test; a reboot undoes it. The RTC alarm cannot be the way back: if the RTC wake does not reach the GIC out of s2idle the phone sleeps for good, which looks the same as a hang. A bite resets the SoC; whether it reaches a normal boot and whether ramoops survives it is what the dry run measures.

brief: A 30 s watchdog fuse resets an idle or hung surya and it boots by itself; the BT-blocked s2idle hang reproduced at once (no log); pstore does not survive the reset
question: Does the watchdog way back work (idle, through a suspend entry, in the hanging cycle), and what log survives?
found: Yes. Idle: reset in 31 s, phone back in ~1.5 min with no hands. Probe (Bluetooth on, s2idle 3 s): the patched qcom_wdt kept counting through the suspend and bit 31 s after arming. The cycle with Bluetooth blocked and a 15 s sleep hung again right at suspend entry (the journal ends at the cycle marker, no PM: suspend entry line, suspend_stats 0/0) and the watchdog reset the phone 30 s after arming, back in under a minute more, no hands. The qcom watchdog counts 32 s at most (BusyBox -T 50 is EINVAL; the default 30 s holds), so a cycle's sleep is at most 15 s. pstore/ramoops stayed empty after every reset (the reset does not keep it); the persistent journal, synced before the arm, is the log that survives up to the last second before the hang. The PMIC RTC cannot be set.

brief: The suspend wake is irq 158 (GPIO 41, the UART RX line, the serial's dedicated wake irq), not 157; the serial's power/wakeup is its mainline switch
question: What ends surya's s2idle at once with Bluetooth up, and what do mainline and others do for a qca UART Bluetooth across suspend?
found: Measured 2026-11-17 on 7.1.0-sm7150-calls+ with ftrace and a kprobe on pm_system_irq_wakeup (suspend-wake-arm-trace.sh in the material): s2idle was ended by irq 158 ('88c000.serial:wakeup', msmgpio 41, edge), armed by dev_pm_arm_wake_irq in the late phase because the platform device 88c000.serial has power/wakeup enabled (qcom_geni_serial sets device_init_wakeup and dev_pm_set_dedicated_wake_irq when the DT gives a second interrupt: the RX pin). The main irq 157 (GIC 636) fires 6 times at the end of qca_suspend, which waits up to 2 s for the chip's sleep indication (hci_qca.c); no 'nobody cared' appeared in these tries. Mainline source read (torvalds/linux master): uart_suspend_port keeps the irq wake only if the tty device serial0 may wakeup (here disabled); hci_qca qca_wakeup() returns device_may_wakeup of the serdev controller and the Bluetooth core then arms a passive scan for suspend, so an RX edge from the chip is a wake by design; the switch is the serial's power/wakeup, a plain sysfs file. With it off for a cycle, s2idle ends by the RTC alarm (RTC counted 7 s for 5 asked, 7 s for 5, 17 s for 15) with hci0 up and scanning after. Not read this time: what postmarketOS ships for qca Bluetooth across suspend (only the earlier note of its hook stopping Bluetooth for the Pixel 3a FastRPC crash). The earlier hang on resume was seen with Bluetooth blocked; not reproduced with it unblocked and wakeup off.

brief: Phone tests are small executables printing one line per case; nobody compiles on the device; upstream pmOS covers only initramfs tests today, so we keep their shape and own the runner
question: How are tests organised, shipped and provisioned on Linux phones (postmarketOS, bootrr, LAVA, CI-tron, systemd), where do rust-script tests plus a bundle crate fit, and should we build fully on postmarketOS upstream?
found: postmarketOS (postmarketos-test subpackages, initramfs hook), bootrr, LAVA and CI-tron share one shape: a test is a small executable, a thin runner prints one pass/fail/skip line per case, the lab collects the lines, device facts live as data. Nobody compiles on the device. rust-script compiles on first run and needs rust+cargo on the phone (Alpine aarch64: 72 MiB download, 206 MiB installed plus gcc/musl-dev/llvm-libs, network for crates): fine on the lab, poor on a phone. A bundle crate that depends on tests (nextest discovery, inventory/linkme) is sound as design but unproven on aarch64 musl; one binary per test found by directory gives the same independence. Provisioning: an apk gives versions, uninstall and signatures at the price of a key and a repository (ours is published); a lab push is fast and leaves no version record. UPSTREAM (checked 2026-11-17; their sites now redirect to nura.eco): MRs on their GitLab with Alpine-style commit rules and approval rules; on-device tests are postmarketos-test-* subpackages run by an initramfs hook that halts the boot; only kernel/initramfs tests work today, boot and system tests (modem, Wi-Fi, audio, sleep - what we need) are not built; their farm is a CI-tron gateway with one OnePlus 6T, joining is token-gated and undocumented; Python is host-side only (pipeline generation, pmbootstrap) and costs nothing on the phone. brief: Pixel 2 in fastboot, read only: unlocked, A/B both slots successful, stock A/B layout, old bootloader with no fastbootd; which Android sits on it is not known yet
question: What does the Pixel 2's bootloader say about the phone, and does Android still sit on it, judged from read-only variables only?
found:
Measured with `fastboot getvar all` (nothing flashed, booted or set): product walleye, hw-revision MP1, boot-mode FASTBOOT, unlocked yes, secure yes, kernel uefi, bootloader mw8998-003.0085.00, baseband g8998-00034-2006052136, slot-count 2, current-slot a, both slots successful=yes unbootable=no retry-count 0, max-download-size 512 MiB, avb 1.0.0 with user-settable key set, battery 4344 mV. Partitions listed with a size: boot_a/b 32 MiB raw, system_a/b 2560 MiB ext4, vendor_a/b 500 MiB ext4, userdata about 53 GiB ext4. is-userspace, slot-suffixes, snapshot-update-status and the sizes of vbmeta, dtbo and modem are not offered: an old bootloader, no fastbootd.
Inference: both slots carry the flags Android's boot control leaves after a good boot, and the partition table is the stock A/B layout, so an Android has run on each slot; userdata of 53 GiB fits the 64 GB model. Which Android, whether it still boots and whether userdata holds data is not known yet - the bootloader cannot say.
Not known yet: whether `fastboot boot` accepts a kernel built by us, and what it does afterwards; every Android reference measurement (sleep current, audio levels, sensors, boot time), backlog google-walleye-lab/android-reference-walleye - it needs the author to boot slot a, enable USB debugging and say when the phone is at the home screen; the paragraph is in the material README.

brief: What the vendor's GPL kernel says walleye's hardware is: Samsung S6E3FA5 panel, Synaptics touch, WCD934x + TAS2557, DRV2624, PMI8998 charger and gauge, NQ NFC, WCN3990, sensors behind the SLPI
question: Which chip is each part of the Pixel 2 (walleye) and how is it wired, by Google's GPL wahoo kernel device tree and the mainline port's tree?
found:
Read from the LineageOS copy of Google's wahoo kernel (4.4, branch lineage-22.2) and kcxt/linux-wahoo wahoo/5.17; observed facts only, nothing copied; table in research/google-walleye/2026-11-17/vendor-kernel-hardware-inventory.md.
Walleye is the HTC-built half of the pair: its files are under dts/htc/ and called "muskie"; one base plus one of two overlays by board revision (xa/xb/xc or xd/xe/a; our MP1 maps to one of them - not known yet). SoC MSM8998 v2.1 with PM8998, PMI8998 and PM8005.
Parts: panel Samsung S6E3FA5 5.0 in 1080x1920 command mode, 4 DSI lanes, reset GPIO94, TE GPIO10, rails PM8998 L14 1.8 V and L22 3.0 V, backlight by DCS (no WLED), always-on modes. Touch Synaptics DSX at I2C 0x20 on the BLSP1 QUP5 bus (GPIO87/88), IRQ GPIO125, reset GPIO89. Audio: WCD934x "Tavil" codec on SLIMbus, TI TAS2557 stereo speaker amp at I2C 0x4d, no jack; NXP TFA98xx amps are in the tree but disabled. Haptics TI DRV2624 (LRA 155 Hz, I2C 0x5a, reset GPIO95). LED: TI LP5562 on early revisions, PMI8998 RGB on later. Charger: PMI8998 SMB2 with Type-C PD, TPS61099 for USB host power, NXP PTN36241G redriver. Fuel gauge: PMI8998 FG gen3 with HTC battery module, 2700 mAh, 4.4 V. NFC: NXP NQ-class at 0x28 plus PN81A secure element on SPI. Fingerprint FPC1020 family (IRQ GPIO86, reset GPIO128). Wi-Fi and Bluetooth: Qualcomm WCN3990 (Bluetooth HCI on BLSP1 UART3). Cameras: two CCI sensors, rear with autofocus, OIS, EEPROM and flash, laser ranger at I2C 0x29; the sensor chips are not named in the tree (public specs: Sony IMX362 rear, IMX179 front). Pixel Visual Core ("Easel") on PCIe 0 with a BCM15602 PMIC and SPI. Storage UFS. Sensors (IMU, magnetometer, barometer, light, Hall) are not in the application processor's tree: the SLPI sensor-hub DSP owns them, firmware proprietary.
For a phone with no display: stock describes a RAM console (ramoops) at 0xa1100000, 2 MiB, plus an alternate at 0xa3800000; the mainline port uses 0xa1810000 instead and boots with console on ttyMSM1 (BLSP2 UART1) and a USB-gadget serial ttyGS0 - which address survives a reset on this phone is not known yet.
The mainline port's walleye file is 13 lines and sets no panel (the shared file's panel is taimen's LG one), and enables UFS, USB peripheral, one DSI, GPU, Wi-Fi, SLPI and ADSP, regulators - nothing for touch, audio, haptics, NFC, gauge, charger, cameras, sensors.
Not known yet: camera and sensor chips on walleye itself, touch controller model, codec exact part, fingerprint wiring, Active Edge sensing, UART test pads, which overlay MP1 uses.

question: How did others boot Linux on the Pixel 2 family (boot image, A/B, fastboot boot, dtbo), what boots, and how did they reach a phone with no display?
found:
Only the Pixel 2 XL (taimen) is reported to have booted mainline, by kcxt (Caleb Connolly) on an out-of-tree 5.10 to 5.17 fork, 2020 to 2022: black screen, USB networking to a shell, flashing works; a March 2021 mainline submission shows no sign of being merged. Detail and URLs in research/google-walleye/2026-11-17/how-others-booted-wahoo.md.
Not known yet: whether this phone's bootloader accepts `fastboot boot` of our image; the dtbo id walleye needs (the README is XL only; changing dtbo writes to the phone); whether `fastboot oem uart enable` only sets a RAM flag or writes something (until known, it is a change to the phone); the boot header version; slot handling for a Linux boot; any report for the small Pixel 2 booting mainline.
Ways forward: (1) read walleye's dtbo overlay ids without writing (from Android if it boots, or Google's factory image, a proprietary download - decision needed); (2) try a first `fastboot boot` of a kernel with appended dtb and a USB-gadget serial console once devlab's fastboot mode exists; (3) build the USB-C debug cable and enable the UART only after a decision on the oem command.

brief: Android on the Pixel 2, read only: LineageOS 15 on stock vendor, 37 sensors, 12 s to system ready; sleep current and audio levels not known yet
question: What does Android do on the Pixel 2 as the author left it - build, sensors, battery, boot time, audio - measured read-only, with nothing installed or changed?
found:

brief: First boot: v0 boot.img, dtb appended with qcom,msm-id, no bootargs in the dts, USB 2.0 gadget instead of a display; whether fastboot boot works with a mainline dtb and the dtbo is not known
question: What does a first mainline boot of the Pixel 2 need, and what can and cannot fastboot boot do on this bootloader?
found:
Image: boot header v0, base 0x0, kernel offset 0x8000, ramdisk 0x1000000, tags 0x100, page 4096 - verified by porthole against the stock TAIMEN boot.img; LineageOS's wahoo board config says tags 0x01E00000 / ramdisk 0x02000000 instead: two sets are reported, walleye's own stock boot.img header decides (not read yet). Boot partition is 32 MiB (getvar boot_a 0x2000000), max-download-size 0x20000000: size is no limit. The DTB is appended to the kernel; it must carry qcom,msm-id = <0x124 0x20001> (taimen has it, kcxt's walleye does not).
Cmdline (porthole): clk_ignore_unused ignore_loglevel panic=10 earlycon=msm_serial_dm,0xc1b0000 qcom_wdt.arm_on_probe=1 watchdog.open_timeout=300 reboot=w; kcxt adds console=ttyGS0,115200. No bootargs/stdout-path in the DTS: ABL appends the boot.img cmdline with fdt_appendprop_string, and a pre-existing bootargs hides it.
Display: command-mode panels, so no scanned-out framebuffer for simple-framebuffer; the first sign of life must be USB. Path: dwc3 peripheral, high-speed only, SuperSpeed PHY dropped, qcom,select-utmi-as-pipe-clk, assigned-clock-rates 19.2/60 MHz (works on taimen); initramfs with a configfs gadget (ACM console + RNDIS/ECM) and telnet/ssh on 172.16.42.1 (devlab's address). pstore: ramoops 0xa1810000/0x200000; a cold reset scrambles it, so the warm-reset/watchdog parameters matter. UART: the Pixel debug cable (see google-walleye-how-others-booted; fastboot oem uart enable is a change to the phone, undecided).
Bootloader (keeper's read-only getvar, google-walleye-bootloader-first-look): mw8998-003.0085.00, hw-revision MP1, unlocked, A/B both slots successful, avb_version 1.0.0, kernel:uefi, no fastbootd.
fastboot boot: TWRP's own instructions for walleye use it (xdaforums), but another report could not boot TWRP that way, and nobody reports a mainline kernel booted from RAM on any Pixel 2: NOT known. Also not known: whether ABL applies the stock dtbo of the active slot to a mainline DTB (taimen's bootloader refuses a kernel unless dtbo holds overlay id 2704 - kcxt's README, taimen only; porthole flashes its own stub into slot b), and what vbmeta/AVB does to an unsigned image on an unlocked phone. One try through devlab (walleye-first-fastboot-boot) answers all three; a refusal is an answer, and the stub dtbo is a write (the author's decision; backlog walleye-dtbo-overlay-id).

brief: Clean room with agents works as an input wall (observer, scrubber, implementer, spec rows with evidence); walleye needs it for few MSM8998 parts; GPL vendor source needs none
question: How is clean-room reverse engineering best done with AI agents, and how should walleye's bring-up apply it?
found: Agents are now near-human at reading binaries (arXiv 2610.14960; 2608.11469 SRE-Bench: best agents solve ~27-32% of realistic ones), but no paper yet covers clean-room hardware bring-up; the practice does. AI "clean rooms" (ArtCraft: a rule on inputs; chardet 7.0: disputed) cannot prove the wall by the model's mind, only by what it was shown - so use an INPUT wall: observer (traces on the stock system, GPL vendor kernel source, public specs) writes spec rows with evidence kind + hash; a separate scrubber checks them for expression; the implementer sees only accepted rows, public specs and mainline; commits cite spec ids; per-session input log and taint register. Tools: mmiotrace/ftrace/dynamic debug/regmap/QMI logs/debugfs on the running stock system (Nouveau, Asahi m1n1 tracing, freedreno), never disassembly or vendor binaries (Asahi: 'without looking at the code'). Walleye: most MSM8998 parts are upstream and need no clean room; likely only panel init, sensor hub, audio calibration/topology, camera, vendor protocols. GPL vendor kernel (android-msm-wahoo, kcxt/linux-wahoo) is read and ported with licence kept - no clean room. EFF: clean room is good practice, not a legal requirement; no court has ruled on AI clean rooms. Not legal advice. Full proposal, table of parts and record design in the material.

brief: With the audio DSP stopped - or all three DSPs - a measured cycle still counts cxsd 0, aosd 0, ddr 0: the audio DSP is not what holds the SoC

Measured 2026-11-17 on the kept kernel (7.1.0-sm7150-calls+, patched qcom_wdt), cycle 15 bt-on, as systemd-run units, nothing polled during a cycle.

brief: Why a failed fastboot boot flipped the Pixel 2's slots, how to restore, how to keep tries from flipping them
question: Why did two fastboot boot tries change the A/B state, how do we restore it, how do we keep tries from flipping it, and should tries run on slot b?
found:
Probable, not proven: the Pixel 2's bootloader is Qualcomm-derived ABL (Google's build is not public). In Qualcomm's ABL source (CAF pie mirror, QcomModulePkg FastbootCmds.c, PartitionTableUpdate.c, avb/VerifiedBoot.c), `fastboot boot` runs LoadImageAndAuth on the active slot; when that fails, HandleActiveSlotUnbootable sets slot a's unbootable flag (leaving successful set - the odd pair we saw), makes b active because b is successful, and cold-resets before the reply (our "Status read failed"). So our kernel probably never ran, and panic=10 is not the cause. `fastboot boot` does not decrement retry-count; a kernel crash falls back to a normal boot of the stock boot partition; a slot that is successful=yes is never counted down.
set_active X (ABL source): makes the slot active at priority 3, retry 7, clears unbootable and successful; swaps the a/b partition-type GUIDs and switches the UFS boot LUN: metadata only, undone by set_active back. a stays successful=no until Android on a marks itself good. `--slot` is ignored by `boot`.
Pixel 2 reports: loops end in "Slot Unbootable: Load Error", fixed by set_active (UBports forum 5639); after 7 unsuccessful boots the bootloader switches slot (pmaports MR 3190); the Pixel 2 XL bootloader refuses a kernel unless dtbo holds overlay id 2704 (kcxt dtbo README) - the likely real cause of the failed authentication, unconfirmed for walleye.
Not known yet: the real failure point; why try a stayed in fastboot and whether it changed flags; why b shows retry 0 after the switch; whether Google's ABL matches Qualcomm's.
Ways: leave flags and try on b (no write; if b is flagged too, set_active is the way out); set_active a now (a stays successful=no, the next failed try flips again); set_active before each try (a write per try); flash a stub dtbo to the active slot (a write, no known way back: the stock dtbo cannot be read back by fastboot); image changes (os_version 0 in our header untested).

brief: Pixel 2 Load Error: format matches what Pixel 3 ABL accepts; likely causes are the dtbo overlay merge, missing board-id/pmic-id, slot state, the os word - a control image first
question: What does the Pixel 2 bootloader dislike in our boot images (Load Error), from public sources, and which variants should be tried next?
found:
What is: four images, one kernel/dtb/initramfs, all v0 with the dtb appended to a gzipped Image (Image.gz+dtb). a (taimen offsets, os word 0) got "Booting OKAY" then silence; b (LineageOS offsets) first left fastboot (Android came back on slot b), later Load Error; c and d (a, b plus os_version 8.1.0 / patch 2020-01) both Load Error. The only difference between a and c is that header word.

What others show (not the Pixel 2 itself - nobody reports a mainline fastboot boot there):
1. The format is the accepted one. Stock ABL on the same line (Pixel 3) takes a gzipped kernel with the dtb appended in a v0 boot image (U-Boot's board doc), and postmarketOS boots blueline with exactly base 0 / kernel 0x8000 / ramdisk 0x1000000 / tags 0x100 / page 4096 / dtb appended (pmaports deviceinfo). Two differences from our images: pmaports sets second offset 0 (we use 0xf00000; second is empty, so it should not matter) and no os_version/patch level at all. So "header v0 vs what ABL expects" and "Image.gz-dtb vs Image+dtb" are not the likely cause; the os word is, if anything, the one thing we added that pmaports does not have.
2. ABL, not the kernel, picks and patches the dtb (Inoki, MSM8998 Nokia 8): DeviceTreeAppended scans the appended blobs and DeviceTreeCompatible matches qcom,msm-id, qcom,board-id and qcom,pmic-id. Our dts carries only msm-id (0x124 0x20001, as kcxt's taimen, which boots with msm-id alone); it has no board-id or pmic-id. Whether walleye's ABL accepts that is not known; the stock walleye dtb's ids are not read yet (not in the public sources reached today).
3. The bootloader merges a dtbo overlay into the dtb before the kernel starts (AOSP DTO). kcxt found the taimen bootloader refuses a mainline kernel unless the dtbo partition holds an overlay with id 2704, and flashes a stub. Stock overlays patch downstream nodes a mainline base does not have, so a failed merge is the best-fitting reading of an immediate "Load Error" that comes from the bootloader after the transfer. Not proven for walleye: the dtbo of slot b is an older LineageOS build's, its overlay table not read.
4. "Load Error" is not proof the image is bad. Known-good TWRP for walleye got the same words from fastboot boot (Android SE), and one XDA report says it appeared randomly and went away on restart. Our slot flags (a unbootable, current b) were left by the first try; whether they feed the refusal is not known.
5. "Booting OKAY" then silence (a) means the bootloader sent its OK and a later step failed or the kernel died before any sign of life; it is a different outcome from Load Error, and a is the only image that got it. The os word turning OKAY into Load Error says the refusal is sensitive to the header word - the likeliest reason is the bootloader comparing the os_version/patch level with the active slot's recorded one (not read anywhere; unknown).

Ranked causes (each has a try that tells it apart): (H1) overlay merge fails against a mainline base, so a stub dtbo or a dtb that survives the stock overlay is needed - only fixable by a write (dtbo_b stub) or by finding that slot b's dtbo is not the cause; (H2) dtb ids: msm-id only, no board-id/pmic-id; free to test on the host; (H3) state: slot flags or random Load Error; test with a control image; (H4) header word: only os word 0 passes, so keep 0.
Control first: a stock-format image known to boot on walleye (LineageOS or TWRP recovery for walleye, public) through the same fastboot boot path. If the control also gets Load Error, the cause is the phone's state and no image change helps; if it boots, the cause is in our image and the variants below tell which part. The control is a try, not a write.
Not read yet and worth reading without writing: walleye's stock boot.img header and dtb ids from a public LineageOS wahoo build (host only), slot b's dtbo overlay ids (pstore/Android adb read - keeper only).

brief: SH0 is a keepalive LLCC BCM; its sleep residual is a TAG_ALWAYS consumer (QUP/uart8), not a latch; AOP QMP wiring equals sm8150, no-ack unexplained
question: What is SH0 x=1,y=3, who votes it, what do SDM845/SM8150/SC7180 do, and why does the AOP not ack QMP?
found:
SH0 is not a holder someone took; it is a keepalive BCM. In mainline sm7150.c, bcm_sh0 is "SH0", keepalive, node qns_llcc, identical to sdm845, sm8150 and sc7180 (the sc7180 Acer Aspire 1 reaches cxsd/aosd/ddr counts with the same definition). bcm-voter.c forces keepalive BCMs to x=y=1 (or enable_mask) only in the AMC and WAKE buckets. The SLEEP bucket is aggregated from consumers' tags only, so a sleep-set SH0 x=1,y=3 means a consumer whose tag includes SLEEP (QCOM_ICC_TAG_ALWAYS = AMC|WAKE|SLEEP) has a path through qns_llcc with a tiny bandwidth. In sm7150.dtsi the candidates are the QUP nodes, which use TAG_ALWAYS interconnects (one serial toward gem_noc SLAVE_LLCC, near line 1259), the crypto engine (ALWAYS to EBI, line 460), and uart8 serial@a88000 (the debug UART), which the recorded cycles show at avg 1 peak 1 across suspend. The owner is a DT tag on a consumer, not a firmware latch.
Whether the SH0 sleep vote blocks aosd is NOT known yet: no source shows the sleep-set contents of the Aspire 1 or any SM7150-class phone; SH0 is only the sole non-zero sleep entry on surya, which makes it the cheapest subtraction.
QMP: the aoss_qmp node (c300000, spi 389, mboxes apss_shared 0, apss_shared at 17c00000) is identical to sm8150 and sc7180, so the wiring in the tree is not the difference. Open succeeds, every send times out: the AOP does not clear the length word after the kick; qmp_send gives no other signal. Downstream wiring (irq-reg-base 17c0000c, mask 1) could not be confirmed from a source this session - not known yet. QMP matters only for the aoss prevent knobs (cx_mol, ddr_mol; hypothesis 5, unlikely) and is not on the path to the SH0 owner.
Read from the tree at kernel-rc3; nothing on the phone was touched.
